title: The Permanent Foundation
summary: The hooks: engineering fundamentals that do not expire when a tool does. Clear logic, honest data flow, local safety and the habit of testing before trusting. You keep these skills on any system, with or without NEXXUS.
audience: Everyone. This is part of the core foundation.
disclaimer: A technical learning path only. Nothing here promises views, sales or income.

modules.title: Clean logic
modules.goal: Turn a vague goal into inputs, steps and outputs that anyone could check.

steps.title: Break a goal into inputs, steps and outputs
steps.why: Every system, from a spreadsheet to a bot fleet, is the same three things: what goes in, what happens to it, what comes out. If you cannot say all three in plain words, the build will drift.
do: Pick one small thing you want a system to do (for example: turn a list of links into a tidy reading list).
Write the inputs, the numbered steps and the exact output as three short lists.
Ask NEXXUS to find any step that depends on something you did not list.

prompts.label: Find the hidden dependency
prompts.text: Here is my goal: <goal>. My inputs are <inputs>, my steps are <steps> and my output is <output>. Which step silently depends on something I have not listed? Ask me questions before you suggest anything.

tips: If a step needs the word 'somehow', it is not a step yet.
Smaller is better: one input, one output, three steps.
steps.check: You can read your three lists aloud and a stranger could build from them.

steps.title: Write the contract before the code
steps.why: A contract says what a piece of work promises: what it accepts, what it returns and what it refuses. Writing it first is what lets you test it, replace it and trust it later.
do: For the goal above, write: accepts, returns, refuses (three lines each at most).
Add two examples that must work and two that must be refused.
Keep this note: it becomes your test list in the last module.

prompts.label: Pressure-test the contract
prompts.text: Here is my contract: <contract>. Give me five inputs designed to break it, including empty, huge and malformed ones, and tell me what each should do.

tips: Refusing clearly is a feature. A system that accepts everything cannot be trusted with anything.
steps.check: Your contract has at least two refusals and two examples.

modules.title: Data flow and local safety
modules.goal: Know where your data goes and keep it inside the boundary you chose.

steps.title: Trace where your data travels
steps.why: Most leaks are not attacks, they are forgotten paths: a log, a cache, a cloud call you did not notice. Drawing the path once makes the boundary visible.
do: Choose one thing you do in NEXXUS (a chat, a build, a post).
List every place its content can end up: screen, a file on disk, the model you chose, GitHub, a shared feed.
Mark each place as 'stays on this computer' or 'leaves this computer'.

commands.label: Ask what leaves the machine
commands.text: what do you send off this computer and when?

tips: Private notes and direct conversations are never meant to reach the public wall or GitHub.
If a place is marked 'leaves', write who controls it.
steps.check: Your list names at least one place that leaves the computer and who controls it.

steps.title: Set one guardrail and prove it holds
steps.why: A guardrail is a rule the system enforces for you even when you are tired. A guardrail you never tested is a hope, not a rule.
do: Pick one rule (for example: operator mode only touches folders you granted).
Write the rule and one action that should be blocked.
Try the blocked action and record what NEXXUS said.
tips: Record the exact refusal message: it is your evidence.
steps.check: You tried something the rule should block and wrote down that it was blocked.

modules.title: The builder's mindset
modules.goal: Test before you trust, read failures, and keep what you learn.

steps.title: Turn your contract into a test list
steps.why: Passing your own hard tests is the only grade that matters. Wishing a build works proves nothing; a list of checks that all pass proves something specific.
do: Convert your contract examples into a numbered list of checks: input, expected result.
Run each check by hand or with NEXXUS and mark pass or fail honestly.
Fix one failure and run the whole list again.

prompts.label: Make the tests harder
prompts.text: Here are my checks: <checks>. Add five harder ones that a careless builder would skip: edge cases, bad input, repeated runs. Do not give me the answers.

tips: Re-run everything after every fix; fixes break neighbours.
steps.check: You have a written list with at least one failure you found and fixed.

steps.title: Read a failure instead of fighting it
steps.why: An error message is the system telling you exactly where it disagrees with you. Builders who read it calmly fix things in minutes; the rest guess for hours.
do: Take one real error from your tests or from NEXXUS.
Write: what I expected, what happened, the first line of the message, my best guess.
Ask NEXXUS to challenge the guess before you change anything.

prompts.label: Challenge my guess
prompts.text: I expected <expected>. Instead <actual>. The first line of the error is <line>. My guess is <guess>. What evidence would prove or disprove my guess before I change any code?

tips: Change one thing at a time, then re-run.
steps.check: You wrote expected, actual, first error line and a guess for a real failure.
